clinicalPearls: Peyronie disease is an acquired fibrotic disorder of the tunica albuginea of the penis, producing a palpable plaque, penile curvature, and sometimes pain, deformity, and shortening
It typically presents in middle-aged men and can cause difficulty with penetration and considerable psychological distress
The disease has two phases: an active (acute) phase with pain and evolving deformity, and a stable (chronic) phase in which the curvature and plaque have plateaued
Erectile dysfunction commonly coexists and should be assessed, as it influences both distress and treatment choice
It is associated with penile trauma or microtrauma during intercourse and with other fibrosing conditions such as Dupuytren contracture, as well as with diabetes
Diagnosis is largely clinical from the history and palpation of the plaque, supplemented by objective assessment of curvature, often after inducing an erection
Non-surgical options during the active phase and for milder deformity include oral and injectable therapies and traction, aiming to reduce curvature and stabilise disease

Surgery is reserved for stable disease with functionally significant deformity and includes plication, plaque incision or excision with grafting, or penile prosthesis when erectile dysfunction is also present
Intervention decisions should await disease stability, since operating during the active phase risks recurrence and further change
reference.pathophysiology: Peyronie disease is thought to begin with repetitive microtrauma to the tunica albuginea, most often during sexual activity, in a susceptible individual. The injury triggers an aberrant, exaggerated wound-healing response with local inflammation, fibroblast activation, and deposition of disorganised collagen and elastin. This forms a fibrous, sometimes calcified, plaque that is less elastic than the surrounding tunica. During erection the inelastic segment fails to expand normally, bending the penis toward the plaque and producing the characteristic curvature and deformity. Over time inflammation subsides and the plaque matures and stabilises, marking the transition to the chronic phase.
additionalDifferentials: Congenital penile curvature (present since puberty, no plaque)
Penile cancer or other penile mass
Dorsal vein thrombosis of the penis
additionalInvestigations: Focused history and palpation of the plaque in the flaccid state
Objective measurement of curvature during an induced or photographically documented erection
Penile duplex ultrasound to characterise plaque, calcification, and vascular status where relevant
Assessment of erectile function using validated questionnaires
Evaluation for associated conditions such as diabetes and Dupuytren contracture
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging or atypical penile mass raising concern for malignancy
Acute severe pain with deformity suggesting penile fracture rather than Peyronie disease
Deformity severe enough to prevent intercourse or urinary function
Significant psychological distress or relationship impact
Progressive deformity that has not stabilised, indicating ongoing active disease
reference.prognosis: The natural history is variable: a minority of men improve spontaneously, many stabilise with residual deformity, and a proportion progress. Pain from the active phase usually resolves over time. With appropriate treatment tailored to disease phase and severity, most men can achieve functional improvement, and surgery in stable disease offers reliable correction of significant curvature, though some penile shortening or altered sensation may persist.
pitfalls: Operating during the active, unstable phase and risking recurrence
Overlooking coexisting erectile dysfunction that alters the treatment approach
Mistaking congenital curvature, which lacks a plaque, for Peyronie disease
Failing to address the psychological impact on the patient and partner
Assuming a penile mass is a benign plaque without excluding malignancy when features are atypical
management: Phase-directed approach with reassurance and active surveillance during the active phase, since spontaneous stabilisation or improvement may occur
Intralesional collagenase Clostridium histolyticum injection for stable-phase curvature with a palpable plaque
Penile traction therapy and mechanical adjuncts to preserve length and reduce curvature

Surgical correction once disease is stable, using tunical plication for adequate length, plaque incision or excision with grafting for severe curvature, or penile prosthesis where erectile dysfunction coexists
Concurrent treatment of erectile dysfunction with phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors, as it influences distress and surgical choice
Analgesia to control pain during the active inflammatory phase
Psychosexual counselling for distress and relationship impact, with referral to specialist andrology or urology
